title: The first nativity scene
hookLine: at Greccio, Francis sets up a manger with a real ox and donkey

cards: Christmas night, in a small hill town called Greccio, in Italy. Men and women from the area are climbing toward a spot near the woods, carrying candles and torches that light up the dark.
Friars have come in from other places. Waiting for them is a manger, filled with hay. Beside it stand an ox and a donkey, real ones, breathing in the cold.
And next to the manger stands Francis of Assisi, singing the Gospel in a clear voice.

teach.h: TO SEE IT WITH BODILY EYES.
teach.b: Thomas of Celano, Francis's early biographer, tells why.

Francis asked a man of Greccio named John to help him prepare it, because, in paraphrase, he wanted to see with his own bodily eyes the hardship the baby went through: how he was laid in a manger, how he lay on hay with an ox and a donkey standing by.
Not a painting. Not an idea. A real manger.

Look at the Gospel's own words. Luke, in the King James Version: "she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn."
A manger is a feeding trough. And notice: Luke never mentions an ox or a donkey.

teach.h: THE OX AND DONKEY COME FROM ISAIAH.
teach.b: They come from a line in Isaiah that Christian tradition set beside the birth story: "The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib." At Greccio the two texts stood side by side, in hay and breath.
Then, Celano says, Mass was celebrated over the manger, and Francis preached about the child of Bethlehem, saying the name with great tenderness.
A man there, Celano adds, saw in a vision a child lying still in the manger, and Francis bending to wake him.
Celano reads that as a picture of the whole night: a child who'd been forgotten in many hearts, woken up again. Tradition calls Greccio the first nativity scene.
Whatever came before it, the custom it's remembered for lives on, in cribs set out in churches and homes, some grand, some small enough to sit on a windowsill.

how: Churches and Christian homes often set out a nativity scene, or crib, during Advent and Christmas; some places hold living nativities with people and animals, and some families add the figure of the baby only on Christmas Eve.

games.q: you're Francis, and you want the people of Greccio to see how poor the Christmas child really was. what do you do?
o: set up a real manger, with hay, an ox and a donkey.
preach a long sermon on poverty.
games.why: he asked John of Greccio to prepare a real manger with hay, an ox and a donkey, so he could see it with his own bodily eyes.

practice: If you have a nativity set, take out one piece and set it where you'll see it; if not, set down any small object on purpose, a cup, a stone, a folded cloth, as a place for something to arrive.
If you pray, let it be a manger, an empty place made ready; if you don't, let it stand for something you want to make real, not just think about.

wordCard.voice: Nativity scene. What tradition calls the first one, at Greccio, where Francis set out a real manger, with hay, an ox and a donkey, so people could see the story with their own eyes.

orig.note: Greek: a manger, a feeding trough — the word in Luke 2:7.

carryVoice: Your line: a real manger. Hay, breath, and a story you can see. That's day eight hundred sixteen.
